claims.text: Resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in HEA multilayer coatings is governed by nanoscale multilayer interfaces.
Nanoscale multilayer interfaces act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Nanoscale multilayer interfaces impede diffusion-driven creep deformation.
The multilayer architecture increases the activation energy required for plastic flow relative to a homogeneous coating.
Sharp interfaces can be formed between chemically complex but crystallographically similar nanoscale HEA layers by a process such as magnetron sputtering.
A monolithic coating with the same overall composition and otherwise identical processing provides a control for the effect of multilayer architecture.
Constant-load testing at 600–700 °C for 100–200 hours in an inert atmosphere can probe time-dependent plastic deformation under the proposed conditions.
Multilayer interfaces suppress diffusion-related deformation mechanisms such as dislocation climb.
Interfaces act as pinning centers for dislocation glide and climb.
The homogeneous coating lacks the interface barriers present in the multilayer coating.
The absence of multilayer interface barriers leads to higher creep rates in the homogeneous coating.
The multilayer coating will exhibit lower cumulative creep strain than the composition-matched monolithic coating under the same test conditions.
The proposed interface effect applies where diffusion-mediated creep is active, including temperatures up to approximately 700 °C.
Nanometer-scale layers allow interfaces to impede dislocation dynamics effectively.
Extremely high temperatures or layer coarsening can diminish the effectiveness of the interfaces.
Dislocation pile-ups and interface-stabilized structures are expected in the multilayer coating after creep testing.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in creep strain or creep rate relative to the control would falsify the proposed interface-barrier hypothesis.
